record.original_question: Find a combinatorial interpretation of Seidel matrices that have exactly three distinct eigenvalues.

evidence.quote: More formally, the Seidel matrix S(Γ) equals Jn − In − 2A(Γ).
Problem 3.32. Find a combinatorial interpretation of Seidel matrices with three distinct eigenvalues.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma$ be a simple undirected graph on $n$ vertices with adjacency matrix $A(\Gamma)$. The Seidel matrix of $\Gamma$ is the symmetric $n\times n$ matrix
$$S(\Gamma) = J_n - I_n - 2A(\Gamma),$$
where $J_n$ is the all-ones matrix and $I_n$ is the identity matrix. Equivalently, $S(\Gamma)$ has $0$ on the diagonal, $-1$ in entry $(i,j)$ when $i\sim j$ in $\Gamma$, and $+1$ when $i\neq j$ and $i\not\sim j$. Two graphs on the same vertex set are called Seidel-switching equivalent if their Seidel matrices are conjugate by a diagonal $\pm 1$ matrix; the Seidel spectrum is an invariant of the switching class.

Provide a combinatorial interpretation (in terms of the structure of the graph, its switching class, or associated combinatorial/geometric objects such as equiangular line systems, two-graphs, designs, or regular structures) characterizing exactly those Seidel matrices $S(\Gamma)$ that have exactly three distinct eigenvalues.
artifact.status_search_result: No general combinatorial characterization is known. Partial progress has been made: Seidel matrices with three distinct eigenvalues are closely connected to systems of equiangular lines and to regular two-graphs, and complete enumerations have been carried out for small orders (n ≤ 23). Recent work (e.g., on determinants of Seidel matrices, regular graphs in the switching class, and split graphs with few Laplacian eigenvalues) addresses related subcases, but a full combinatorial interpretation remains open.

status_evidence.claim: Only partial enumerative results are known; no general combinatorial characterization is given.
